assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Ammonia
items.clue: The compound NH3 made by the Haber process.

items.label: Raw material
items.clue: A substance fed into an industrial process.

items.label: NPK fertiliser
items.clue: Contains compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

items.label: Formulation
items.clue: A mixture made in fixed proportions so that it does a job.

questions.stem: What is manufactured directly by the Haber process?

options.text: Ammonia, which is then used to make nitrogen fertilisers
Ammonium nitrate, ready for spreading onto farm fields
Nitrogen and hydrogen, made by breaking down ammonia
Nitrogen and hydrogen, drawn straight from the air

questions.explanation: The Haber process manufactures ammonia, and that ammonia is used to produce nitrogen-based fertilisers.

questions.stem: Which pair of gases are the raw materials for the Haber process?

options.text: Nitrogen and oxygen gas
Nitrogen and hydrogen
Hydrogen and water
Hydrogen and oxygen

questions.explanation: The specification states that the raw materials for the Haber process are nitrogen and hydrogen.

questions.stem: A student is asked to give a source of the nitrogen used in the Haber process. Which answer is correct?

options.text: It is obtained from the air, together with the hydrogen
It is obtained by heating ammonium salts in large vessels
It is obtained from the air, which is about 78% nitrogen
It is obtained by electrolysis of concentrated brine

questions.explanation: Air is the source of the nitrogen and is about 78% nitrogen by volume.

questions.stem: Which is the usual industrial source of the hydrogen used in the Haber process?

options.text: Electrolysis of water, which splits it into elements
The air, as hydrogen is one of the gases present in it
Heating ammonia so that it splits into its elements
Natural gas, which consists mainly of methane

questions.explanation: Hydrogen is obtained from natural gas (methane) or from other hydrocarbons.

questions.stem: Which conditions are used in the Haber process?

options.text: An iron catalyst, 450 degrees C and 20 atmospheres
An iron catalyst, 450 degrees C and 200 atmospheres
A nickel catalyst, 450 degrees C and 200 atmospheres
An iron catalyst, 45 degrees C and 20 atmospheres

questions.explanation: The specification gives an iron catalyst, a high temperature of about 450 degrees C and a high pressure of about 200 atmospheres.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the iron catalyst in the Haber process?

options.text: It increases the yield of ammonia formed at equilibrium
It only speeds up the reaction at 450 degrees C or above
It speeds up the rate at which the equilibrium is reached
It stops the ammonia formed from breaking down again

questions.explanation: The catalyst raises the rate of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium arrives sooner.

questions.stem: The Haber reaction is reversible. What does this mean inside the reactor?

options.text: All the nitrogen and hydrogen react, then some ammonia breaks down
The reaction runs forwards during the day and backwards at night
The ammonia formed can never break down once it is made
Some of the ammonia breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen

questions.explanation: The specification states that the reaction is reversible, so some of the ammonia produced breaks down again.

questions.stem: Which equation for the Haber process is written as the specification gives it?

options.text: nitrogen +hydrogen ⇌ammonia
ammonia ⇌nitrogen + hydrogen
nitrogen + hydrogen → ammonia
nitrogen + hydrogen ⇌ ammonium

questions.explanation: This is the word equation exactly as the specification states it, with the double arrow for a reversible reaction.

questions.stem: Which balanced symbol equation represents the Haber process?

options.text: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ NH3
N2 + H2 ⇌ NH3

questions.explanation: Two nitrogen atoms and six hydrogen atoms appear on each side, so the equation is balanced.

questions.stem: The mixture leaving the reactor is cooled. What happens?

options.text: The nitrogen and the hydrogen liquefy and are then drawn off
All three gases liquefy together and are then distilled
The ammonia decomposes back to nitrogen and hydrogen
The ammonia liquefies and is removed from the gas mixture

questions.explanation: On cooling, the ammonia liquefies and is removed, leaving the other two gases behind.

questions.stem: What happens to the nitrogen and hydrogen that have not reacted?

options.text: They are recycled back through the reactor
They are burnt to provide heat for the reactor
They are released into the air as harmless gases
They are cooled and sold as by-products

questions.explanation: The remaining hydrogen and nitrogen are recycled, so the raw materials are not wasted.

questions.stem: A graph shows the rate of the Haber reaction against temperature at a fixed pressure. What does it show?

options.text: The rate falls steadily as the temperature is increased
The rate rises as the temperature is increased
The rate falls as the temperature rises because the yield falls
The rate is highest at the lowest temperatures on the graph

questions.explanation: Higher temperature means more frequent and more energetic collisions, so the rate increases.

questions.stem: A graph shows the percentage yield of ammonia against pressure at 450 degrees C. What is the trend, and why?

options.text: Yield falls, because squashing the gases hinders the reaction
Yield is constant, because pressure only changes the rate
Yield falls, because ammonia is squeezed back into its elements
Yield rises, because there are fewer gas molecules in the ammonia

questions.explanation: Four molecules of gas become two, so raising the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia.

questions.stem: Inside a sealed Haber reactor at equilibrium, what is true?

options.text: Both reactions are still going on at the same rate
Both the forward and reverse reactions have stopped
The amounts of all three gases are now equal
Only the forward reaction is taking place

questions.explanation: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates, so amounts stay constant.

questions.stem: Ammonia is removed from the mixture as it liquefies. What is the effect on the equilibrium?

options.text: There is no effect, since the ammonia has already been made
It shifts towards the ammonia side, so more gas reacts
It shifts back towards the nitrogen and hydrogen instead
It stops the reverse reaction from happening at all

questions.explanation: Removing a product moves the equilibrium to replace it, raising the overall conversion.

questions.stem: Why is the Haber process not run at a much lower temperature than 450 degrees C?

options.text: Because the yield of ammonia would be lower at low temperatures
Because the iron catalyst does not work at all below 450 C
Because the reaction would then be far too slow to use
Because a lower temperature would shift the equilibrium back

questions.explanation: A low temperature gives a better yield but so slow a rate that the plant would be uneconomic.

questions.stem: What is meant by the trade-off between rate of production and position of equilibrium?

options.text: The conditions give the most ammonia per day, not the best yield or the fastest rate
The conditions chosen are simply those that give the fastest possible reaction
The conditions chosen are the ones giving the highest possible yield of ammonia
The catalyst is chosen so that the yield and the rate can both be maximised

questions.explanation: A compromise temperature accepts a lower equilibrium yield in exchange for a workable rate of production.
